explanations.explanation: Flip that one over, friend. Verse 12 says Eli's sons had no regard for the LORD, and verse 13 adds "or for the custom of the priests with the people" (1 Samuel 2:12-13). So the custom was there, and they had no regard for it. The two of them are a long way from honoring it.

Right, friend: they have none. Verse 12 says they had no regard for the LORD, and verse 13 adds "the custom of the priests with the people" (1 Samuel 2:12-13). Picture a recipe card taped to my oven door, and these two just walk right past it.

That's the one, friend. The priest's servant comes with a three-pronged meat fork while the meat is boiling (1 Samuel 2:13). Three prongs! I've got a mustache for hands and even I think that's a lot of fork.

A basin sounds sensible, doesn't it? But the text doesn't mention one. The servant of the priest comes with a three-pronged meat fork while the meat is boiling (1 Samuel 2:13). Sensible tools aren't what this scene is about.

A knife is a fair guess, friend, since we're talking about meat. But verse 13 says the servant comes with a three-pronged meat fork (1 Samuel 2:13). Verse 14 tells where that fork goes next: into the pan, kettle, cauldron or cooking pot (1 Samuel 2:14).

Himself, friend. Verse 14 says the priest would claim for himself whatever the meat fork brought up (1 Samuel 2:14). Whatever came up on those prongs belonged to him. It's a lucky dip where only one person ever wins, and he's the one holding the fork.

The altar sounds like a respectable place for it to go, friend. But verse 14 says the priest would claim "for himself" whatever the fork brought up (1 Samuel 2:14). The catch didn't go anywhere else. That's exactly what makes the scene so troubling.
That's a generous thought, baker, and I like where your heart is. But the text says the priest would claim it for himself (1 Samuel 2:14). Nothing in the verse sends it to anyone else. He keeps it.
Not a few, friend. Verse 14 ends with, "This is how they treated all the Israelites who came to Shiloh." (1 Samuel 2:14). All of them. Not some, not most, ALL.

Right, baker: it's not just a few. Verse 14 says, "This is how they treated all the Israelites who came to Shiloh." (1 Samuel 2:14). The text names no exceptions. Nobody walks out saying, "Funny, they skipped my pot."

Raw. The servant says the priest "will not accept boiled meat from you, but only raw" (1 Samuel 2:15). So a man with a pot already going is asked to hand over meat before it's cooked. Even I let my cookies finish baking before I grab one, friend.

Salted is a smart-sounding guess, since we're talking about meat. But the servant's words are "he will not accept boiled meat from you, but only raw" (1 Samuel 2:15). Raw is the word he uses. The text says nothing about salt.

Dried is a fair guess, friend, but it isn't what the servant says. His words are "he will not accept boiled meat from you, but only raw" (1 Samuel 2:15). So it's raw the priest wants. The text doesn't mention dried meat anywhere in this scene.

explanations.answer: Give it now or I take it by force
explanations.explanation: Yes, and notice there's no negotiating. The man says the fat must be burned first, then you may take whatever you want, and the servant replies, "No, you must give it to me right now. If you refuse, I will take it by force!" (1 Samuel 2:16). I think the man's offer sounds fair, and he got a threat for it. That's not a servant, friend, that's a one-man shakedown.

explanations.answer: Fine but the priest wants extra
explanations.explanation: The servant never says "fine" about anything, friend. He answers, "No, you must give it to me right now…" (1 Samuel 2:16). There's no giving in and no extra, just a demand. The man asked for the fat to be burned first and got a flat no.

explanations.answer: Then the priest will take none
explanations.explanation: That would be a graceful ending, baker, but the servant goes the opposite way. He says, "No, you must give it to me right now. If you refuse, I will take it by force!" (1 Samuel 2:16). Instead of backing off, he threatens. Taking none is about as far from that as you can get.

True, friend, and that's the LORD's own view. Verse 17 says "the sin of these young men was severe in the sight of the LORD" (1 Samuel 2:17). The text doesn't soften it one bit. When the LORD calls something severe, I listen.

It's the other way, baker. Verse 17 says "the sin of these young men was severe in the sight of the LORD" (1 Samuel 2:17). Severe is the word the text uses. It doesn't call it a small slip or a misunderstanding.

Contempt. The verse says they were "treating the LORD’s offering with contempt" (1 Samuel 2:17). Contempt means looking down on something that deserves honor. Every cookie box headed for the Supper gets handled like treasure around here, friend, and this is the opposite.

Care is the opposite of what's going on, friend. Verse 17 says they were "treating the LORD’s offering with contempt" (1 Samuel 2:17). Treating something with care means handling it gently. The fork and the demands in the verses before it show the other side of that.

Fear doesn't fit, friend. Verse 12 says these two had no regard for the LORD, and verse 17 names the sin: they were "treating the LORD’s offering with contempt" (1 Samuel 2:12, 17). Contempt is looking down on something. It's not trembling in front of it.

A little robe, friend. Verse 19 says his mother would make him a little robe and bring it to him when she went with her husband to offer the annual sacrifice (1 Samuel 2:19). Once a year, made for him and brought to him. I think Hannah sewed a whole lot of love into that thing.

A belt is a nice guess, friend, but verse 19 names something else. Each year his mother would make him "a little robe" (1 Samuel 2:19). She brings it when she goes with her husband to offer the annual sacrifice. The text doesn't mention a belt.

Sandals would be useful, baker, but they aren't in the verse. It says his mother would make him "a little robe" and bring it to him (1 Samuel 2:19). That's the gift, and she brings it each year at the annual sacrifice.

Three sons and two daughters, friend. Verse 21 says the LORD attended to Hannah, and she gave birth to three sons and two daughters (1 Samuel 2:21). That comes right after Eli's blessing in verse 20, and the text begins it with "So." Five more children, and somebody's house just got a whole lot louder.
That guess adds up to three children, friend, but verse 21 says Hannah had three sons and two daughters (1 Samuel 2:21). That's five children. It's two more than you picked, and a much fuller house.
Four sons would be a full house, friend, but verse 21 says three sons and two daughters (1 Samuel 2:21). So there were daughters in the count. Five children in all.

Other way around, friend. Eli tells his sons, "No, my sons; it is not a good report I hear circulating among the LORD’s people." (1 Samuel 2:24). What's going around about them is the opposite of good news. Eli says it right to his sons.

Right, baker. Eli says, "it is not a good report I hear circulating among the LORD’s people" (1 Samuel 2:24). Just before that, he asks his sons, "Why are you doing these things?" (1 Samuel 2:23). I think that's a hard conversation for any father.

explanations.answer: No one can step in for him
explanations.explanation: No one, friend, and Eli puts it as a question: "If a man sins against another man, God can intercede for him; but if a man sins against the LORD, who can intercede for him?" (1 Samuel 2:25). He leaves it hanging for his sons to hear. It's a serious one. I think he asks it so they'll stop and think.

explanations.answer: Only Eli can step in for him
explanations.explanation: Eli never says that, friend. He asks, "who can intercede for him?" and he doesn't name himself or anyone else (1 Samuel 2:25). The question is left open. He only says God can intercede when a man sins against another man.

explanations.answer: His family can step in for him
explanations.explanation: Family isn't part of what Eli says, baker. He asks, "who can intercede for him?" about a man who sins against the LORD (1 Samuel 2:25). He doesn't name any helper. The only one he names is God, and that's for a sin against another man.

No, friend. Verse 25 says "they would not listen to their father" (1 Samuel 2:25). Eli asked his question, and the sons didn't take it in. The same verse adds the weight behind it: the LORD intended to put them to death.

Right, baker. The text says "they would not listen to their father, since the LORD intended to put them to death" (1 Samuel 2:25). That's a serious thing to read, and it should be. Eli spoke up, and they didn't listen.

explanations.answer: In favor with the LORD and with man
explanations.explanation: In favor with the LORD and with man, friend. Verse 26 says the boy Samuel "continued to grow in stature and in favor with the LORD and with man" (1 Samuel 2:26). Stature means height, and he keeps growing in that too. I've been the same height since the Millers carved my name into my handle.

explanations.answer: In honor among the city elders
explanations.explanation: City elders are a reasonable guess, friend, since honor sounds grand. But verse 26 says Samuel grew "in favor with the LORD and with man" (1 Samuel 2:26). The text doesn't name any elders. It's favor with the LORD and with people.

explanations.answer: In charge of the priests' servants
explanations.explanation: Being in charge of anybody is a stretch, friend. The text has Samuel ministering before the LORD (1 Samuel 2:18). Then verse 26 says he grew "in favor with the LORD and with man" (1 Samuel 2:26). He isn't put in charge of the servants anywhere in this passage.

Priest. The man of God brings Eli this word from the LORD: "out of all the tribes of Israel I selected your father to be My priest" (1 Samuel 2:27-28). Out of ALL the tribes! That's a pick from a huge crowd, and the LORD did the picking.

Prophet is a fair guess, friend, but the LORD's words through the man of God name a different job: "to be My priest" (1 Samuel 2:27-28). That job comes with offering sacrifices on His altar, burning incense, and wearing an ephod in His presence (1 Samuel 2:28). Those are a priest's duties.

A king is a big job, baker, but that's not what the LORD says. He selected Eli's father "to be My priest, to offer sacrifices on My altar, to burn incense, and to wear an ephod in My presence." (1 Samuel 2:28). That's a priest's work from start to finish. A crown just isn't in this verse.

Sons. The LORD says to Eli, "You have honored your sons more than Me by fattening yourselves with the best of all the offerings of My people Israel." (1 Samuel 2:29). Eli is the one who has to hear that. I think that's a hard thing for a father to take in.

Elders don't appear in the LORD's words here, friend. He says, "You have honored your sons more than Me" (1 Samuel 2:29). The ones named are Eli's own sons. That's who the LORD puts on the other side of the scale.

The servants were busy with that fork back in verse 13, so I see why they came to mind. But the LORD's words say, "You have honored your sons more than Me" (1 Samuel 2:29). Sons are the ones named. Servants don't show up in that sentence.

Half of it, friend. The first half is right: "I will honor those who honor Me." But the LORD goes on, "those who despise Me will be disdained" (1 Samuel 2:30). Disdained, not overlooked. Overlooked would mean ignored, and disdained means looked down on.

Right, and the second half is the catch. The LORD declares, "I will honor those who honor Me, but those who despise Me will be disdained." (1 Samuel 2:30). Disdained, not overlooked. The first half is the good news: those who honor Him get honored.

explanations.answer: They will both die on the same day
explanations.explanation: The same day, friend. The LORD's sign about Hophni and Phinehas is, "They will both die on the same day" (1 Samuel 2:34). That's a heavy word. I think it's hard on Eli to hear it about his own two sons.

explanations.answer: They will be taken captive together
explanations.explanation: Captive is a guess, friend, but the sign the LORD gives is about death: "They will both die on the same day" (1 Samuel 2:34). It names Hophni and Phinehas and says nothing about being taken anywhere. It's a heavy sign, and the text states it plainly.

explanations.answer: They will die many years apart
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite, friend. The LORD's sign is, "They will both die on the same day" (1 Samuel 2:34). Same day, not years apart. It's a heavy word, and it's about Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas.

True, friend. The LORD says, "I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest. He will do whatever is in My heart and mind." (1 Samuel 2:35). After all that heavy talk, here's a different note: a priest who does what the LORD has in mind. And the LORD says He will build him an enduring house.

It goes the other way, baker. Verse 35 says "He will do whatever is in My heart and mind" (1 Samuel 2:35). Not some of it. Whatever. The faithful priest is the one the LORD says He will raise up for Himself.

Priestly. The LORD says they'll plead, "Please appoint me to some priestly office so that I can eat a piece of bread." (1 Samuel 2:36). They're begging for a priestly office, the very kind of work the LORD gave their family in verse 28. I think that's a long way down.

Royal would be a big step up, friend, but verse 36 says "priestly." The plea is, "Please appoint me to some priestly office so that I can eat a piece of bread." (1 Samuel 2:36). They're asking for a place in the priests' work. A palace is not what they ask for.

Military doesn't appear, friend. The plea is, "Please appoint me to some priestly office so that I can eat a piece of bread." (1 Samuel 2:36). It's a priestly office they ask for, and bread is the reason they give. They want the work of a priest, not a soldier's post.
